fixes.explanation: Quaking is the word, friend. David says, "Heal its fractures, for it is quaking." (Psalm 60:2) The land is shaking, and he takes that shaking straight to God. He doesn't keep it to himself.

Beloved is the word, friend. David asks God to "Respond and save us with Your right hand, that Your beloved may be delivered." (Psalm 60:5) He calls them God's beloved right there in the prayer. That's who he wants delivered.
That's it, friend. God says, "Ephraim is My helmet, Judah is My scepter." (Psalm 60:7) A helmet is worn and a scepter is held. Both are pictures of something close to Him.
Not quite, friend. Over Philistia God says, "…I shout in triumph." (Psalm 60:8) There's no weeping in that line. It's a shout of triumph, not sorrow.
That's right, friend. God says, "over Philistia I shout in triumph." (Psalm 60:8) It's a shout of triumph. There's no crying of sorrow in it.
Fortified is right, friend. David asks, "Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?" (Psalm 60:9) A fortified city has defenses built around it. So it's no easy walk in.
Man is the word, friend. David says, "Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless." (Psalm 60:11) He says it plainly. Nobody has to wonder why he's asking God.
Yes, it's the last line, friend. "With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies." (Psalm 60:12) David ends the song with God at the center. Those are the very last words.
I get why you'd lean that way, friend, but this song starts at the bottom of the pan. David says God has rejected them, broken them and been angry (Psalm 60:1). That's where the song begins.

Yes, that's the reason given, friend. God has raised a banner for those who fear Him, "…that they may flee the bow." (Psalm 60:4) The banner is for those who fear Him. The reason given is fleeing the bow.
Resting doesn't show up in these words, friend. God speaks from His sanctuary and begins with "I will triumph!" (Psalm 60:6) Triumph is how those words open.
Wages don't come up in this song, friend. David asks, "Will You no longer march out, O God, with our armies?" (Psalm 60:10) It's about God marching out with the armies.
Heaven isn't what David is knocking, friend. He says, "…for the help of man is worthless." (Psalm 60:11) He's asking God because he calls human help worthless.
